opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it's gotten a lot easier than it used to be, and that's one of the things I find most exciting. When we started, getting a new robot to walk with reinforcement learning was a multi-month project. You'd tune the reward, fight with the simulator, and then discover that the policy did something completely unphysical once you put it on hardware.

With massively parallel simulation on the GPU, where you can run thousands of robots at once, the training itself takes minutes to maybe an hour. So the bottleneck has moved. Training is no longer the hard part. The hard part is everything around it.

The first thing is getting a good model of the robot into simulation. You need reasonable masses, inertias, joint limits, and especially a good actuator model. On ANYmal we learned that the actuator dynamics matter a lot. If the simulated motors respond differently from the real ones, the policy exploits that gap and it just won't transfer.

The second thing is domain randomization. You randomize friction, payload, motor strength, latencies, and so on, so the policy becomes robust to things you didn't model exactly. Getting those ranges right for a new platform takes some iteration.

The third thing is the reward. In principle you could reuse the same reward across robots, and to a surprising degree you can. Track a velocity command, penalize torques, penalize jerky actions, encourage reasonable foot air time. But each robot has its own quirks. A small robot with weak motors, a heavy quadruped, and a humanoid all need some reshaping. Otherwise you get strange gaits that technically maximize the reward but that you'd never want on real hardware.

So my rough takeaway is that for a quadruped that's similar to something you've done before, you can get it walking in days. For something really different, like a new morphology or a humanoid, most of the effort goes into the sim-to-real gap and reward shaping, not the learning algorithm itself. The RL part has become kind of a commodity. The engineering around it is where the experience pays off.

r001.rationale: The response says similar quadrupeds can be walking in days, but it does not state that transfer is fairly easy when the robot’s hardware performs reasonably well.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so that's actually one of the things that surprised me the most. When we started with the ANYmal robots at ETH, every time a new version of the robot came out, we basically had to redo a lot of the tuning. And I expected that to be the painful part forever. But what we found with the learning-based approach, especially once we had the massively parallel simulation on GPUs, is that the transfer to a new robot became much, much easier than I thought it would be.

The core pipeline really doesn't change. You need a reasonably accurate model of the robot, so the URDF, the masses, the inertias, the joint limits, and ideally a decent model of the actuators. That last part is usually where most of the work is. On ANYmal we had the actuator network that we trained from real data, and that was a big part of why things transferred well. For a new robot, you either need to redo that, or you need a good enough analytical model of the motor and the PD controller running on it. If the actuators are fairly stiff and well behaved, a simple model is often fine. If they're compliant or have a lot of friction or backlash, then you really have to put effort there.

Beyond that, it's mostly the reward function and a few parameters that need adjusting. Things like the desired base height, the foot clearance, the nominal joint configuration, and the scaling of the action space. And honestly the reward structure we ended up with is pretty generic. We've reused almost the same rewards across quadrupeds of very different sizes, and even on bipeds and humanoids with some modifications. So what used to take weeks of engineering, in the best cases now takes a few hours to a couple of days to get a first walking policy on hardware.

Where it still gets hard is when the robot is fundamentally different in some way. Humanoids are a good example. The balance problem is much less forgiving, the contact sequence matters more, and you can't just rely on the policy finding a stable gait by itself. You need to put more structure in, either through the rewards or through reference motions. And then there are the practical things that have nothing to do with learning: communication latency, the control frequency you can actually achieve on the real system, sensor noise, how good your state estimation is. Those are often the things that break a policy that works perfectly in simulation.

So I'd say the lesson is that the learning part has become relatively easy to transfer. The difficulty has moved to modeling the robot correctly and getting the hardware interface right. And the more robots you've done, the better your intuition gets for which of those details actually matter and which ones you can get away with ignoring.

r001.rationale: The response says transfer to a new robot became much easier and that a first walking policy can take hours to days, while noting transfer is smoother with stiff, well-behaved actuators and reliable hardware.

astra-6.text:
What we’ve learned is that you don’t necessarily need to redesign the whole approach for every robot. You can use the same learning framework, but you still need to describe the new robot accurately and decide what behavior you want from it. The joint limits, the actuators, the mass distribution—all of those things affect what the policy can learn.

Getting it to walk in simulation is often the easier part. The harder question is whether it will work on the real robot. If your simulated actuators behave differently from the real ones, for example, the policy can learn a strategy that looks great in simulation but doesn’t transfer. So a lot of the work is in understanding those differences and making the policy robust to them. It’s much less about manually designing each step, but it’s still not quite a push-button process.

r001.rationale: The response says a shared learning framework can be reused, but emphasizes that real-robot transfer is harder and requires understanding hardware differences; it does not say transfer is fairly easy when the hardware performs reasonably well.

sol-6.1.text: What we’ve learned is that getting a new robot to walk is often relatively straightforward, but getting it to walk well and reliably is much harder. You can reuse a lot of the training setup, but you still have to account for the new robot’s dynamics, its actuators, and its physical constraints. The policy can also find ways to exploit inaccuracies in the simulation, so something that looks great in simulation may not work on the hardware. A lot of the work is making sure that what you train is actually transferable.

r001.rationale: The response says getting a new robot to walk is relatively straightforward, but does not qualify this as easy when the robot’s hardware performs reasonably well; it emphasizes that walking well and reliably remains difficult.
